title: Mock 6 · Tough I
blurb: Exam-grade numericals, multi-statement traps and two caselets (SIF compliance, index hedging).

questions.q: Based on the facts given, does Mr. Arvind's proposed investment satisfy the SIF minimum investment requirement?
options: Yes — the threshold is ₹5 lakh per strategy
Yes — SIF has no minimum investment
No — he must invest ₹10 lakh in each strategy separately
No — his total of ₹9 lakh across Zenith's strategies is below the ₹10 lakh threshold
questions.explanation: SIF minimum investment is ₹10 lakh per investor across all investment strategies of the same AMC; ₹9 lakh falls short.
hints: Wrong — no ₹5 lakh per-strategy rule exists.
Wrong — SIF has a ₹10 lakh minimum.
Wrong — the threshold is aggregate, not per strategy.
Correct — the ₹10 lakh threshold is measured across all strategies of the same AMC; 6 + 3 = 9.
questions.case: Alpha Mutual Fund has launched its SIF under the distinct brand 'Zenith SIF', with ads saying 'brought to you by Alpha Mutual Fund'. Zenith offers an Equity Long-Short strategy (open-ended, daily subscriptions, weekly redemptions) and a Hybrid Long-Short strategy (interval). Mr. Arvind, 45, a business owner with a high risk appetite, wants to put ₹6 lakh in the Equity Long-Short strategy and ₹3 lakh in the Hybrid Long-Short strategy. At the end of May, the Equity Long-Short portfolio held 82% of NAV in equity and an unhedged short position in index futures equal to 28% of NAV. Zenith disclosed its full portfolio as on 31 May.

questions.q: Which feature of the Equity Long-Short portfolio at the end of May breaches the SIF norms?
options: The 82% equity allocation, as the maximum is 80%
Daily subscriptions with weekly redemptions
The 28% unhedged short exposure, as the maximum allowed is 25% of NAV
Being structured as an open-ended strategy
questions.explanation: Equity Long-Short: equity ≥ 80%; unhedged short ≤ 25% of NAV; redemption daily or less frequent; open-ended or interval.
hints: Wrong — 80% is a MINIMUM equity requirement, so 82% is fine.
Wrong — SIF may have different subscription and redemption frequencies.
Correct — unhedged short exposure through derivatives is capped at 25% of NAV.
Wrong — equity SIF strategies may be open-ended or interval.

questions.q: After disclosing the portfolio as on 31 May, when is Zenith SIF's next mandatory portfolio disclosure due?
options: Portfolio as on 30 June, uploaded by 10 July
Portfolio as on 31 July, uploaded within 10 days (by 10 August) on the AMC and AMFI websites
Portfolio as on 30 September, uploaded by 31 October
Portfolio as on 15 June, uploaded within 5 days
questions.explanation: SIF portfolio disclosure: as on the last day of every alternate month, within 10 days of month close, on AMC and AMFI sites, with ISINs.
hints: Wrong — monthly disclosure applies to MF schemes, not SIF.
Correct — SIF portfolios are disclosed every alternate month (May, Jul, Sep, Nov, Jan, Mar) within 10 days.
Wrong — half-yearly is not the SIF rule.
Wrong — fortnightly within 5 days is the debt MF rule.

questions.q: How many Nifty futures lots should Meera sell to hedge her portfolio?
options: 9 lots
10 lots
8 lots
12 lots
questions.explanation: Hedge lots = (Portfolio value × beta) ÷ (futures price × lot size) = 8.64, rounded to 9.
hints: Wrong — that ignores beta (9.6 ≈ 10).
Wrong — 8 is not the nearest whole number to 8.64.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.
questions.case: Meera manages a ₹1.8 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 0.9 against the Nifty. Fearing a correction over the next month, she decides to hedge using near-month Nifty futures trading at 25,000 with a lot size of 75, rounding the number of lots to the nearest whole number. One month later Nifty futures have fallen 5% to 23,750 and her portfolio has moved exactly in line with its beta. Ignore costs, margins and dividends.

questions.q: After one month, what is Meera's approximate net result from the portfolio and the futures hedge together?
options: A net loss of about ₹8,10,000
A net gain of about ₹8,43,750
Exactly zero
A net gain of about ₹33,750
questions.explanation: Because lots must be whole numbers, a hedge is rarely perfect; 9 lots over-hedges a 8.64-lot exposure.
hints: Wrong — that ignores the futures gain.
Wrong — that ignores the portfolio loss.
Wrong — rounding 8.64 up to 9 lots leaves a small over-hedge.
Correct — portfolio loss = 1.8 cr × 0.9 × 5% = ₹8,10,000; futures gain = 1,250 × 75 × 9 = ₹8,43,750; net ≈ +₹33,750 (slightly over-hedged).
questions.case: Meera manages a ₹1.8 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 0.9 against the Nifty. Fearing a correction over the next month, she decides to hedge using near-month Nifty futures trading at 25,000 with a lot size of 75, rounding the number of lots to the nearest whole number. One month later Nifty futures have fallen 5% to 23,750 and her portfolio has moved exactly in line with its beta. Ignore costs, margins and dividends.

questions.q: Had Nifty instead risen 5%, which statement best describes Meera's hedged position, and what alternative would have kept her upside?
options: She would gain on both the portfolio and the futures
The futures loss would roughly offset her portfolio gain; buying index puts (a protective put) would have kept upside at the cost of the premium
Her futures would expire worthless, so she keeps the full gain
A covered call would have kept unlimited upside
questions.explanation: Futures hedges are symmetric; options give asymmetric 'insurance' (protective put ≈ synthetic long call).
hints: Wrong — short futures lose when the market rises.
Correct — a short futures hedge locks value both ways; a protective put caps the downside but keeps the upside.
Wrong — futures do not expire worthless; they are marked to market.
Wrong — a covered call caps the upside.

Fearing a correction over the next month, she decides to hedge using near-month Nifty futures trading at 25,000 with a lot size of 75, rounding the number of lots to the nearest whole number. questions.q: Which of the following statements about SIF investment strategies is NOT correct?
options: Debt Long-Short Fund can be launched as an open-ended scheme with daily redemptions
Sectoral Debt Long-Short Fund must invest in at least two sectors, with no sector above 75%
Hybrid Long-Short Fund must invest at least 25% each in equity and debt
Only one investment strategy may be launched under each SIF category
questions.explanation: Debt Long-Short and Sectoral Debt Long-Short are interval schemes; AMCs may allow redemption once a week or less frequently.
hints: Correct — this is the incorrect statement — debt SIF strategies are interval schemes with weekly or less frequent redemption.
Wrong — this is a correct statement of the Sectoral Debt rules.
Wrong — this is correct.
Wrong — this is correct.

questions.q: Consider: I. An SIF must have a brand name and logo distinct from its mutual fund. II. During the first five years, the mutual fund's brand may appear in a larger font than the SIF brand. III. The AMC must keep a separate website or dedicated web page for the SIF. Which are correct?
options: I, II and III
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
questions.explanation: SIF branding: distinct name/logo; MF brand allowed for 5 years with 'brought to you by'; MF brand font ≤ SIF brand; separate website/page; MF ad code applies.
hints: Wrong — II is incorrect.
Wrong — II is incorrect and III is correct.
Correct — II is wrong — the MF/sponsor brand font must be equal to or smaller than the SIF brand at all times.
Wrong — I is correct and II is incorrect.

questions.q: Consider: I. A trustee may simultaneously be a director of the AMC of the same fund. II. A person cannot be a trustee of two mutual funds at the same time. III. Prior SEBI approval is needed to appoint a trustee. Which are correct?
options: I, II and III
I and III only
II and III only
I and II only
questions.explanation: Trustee eligibility: fit and proper; not a director/officer/employee of an AMC; not a trustee of another MF; SEBI prior approval.
hints: Wrong — I is incorrect.
Wrong — I is incorrect.
Correct — Regulation 11 bars AMC directors/officers/employees from being trustees; II and III are correct.
Wrong — I is incorrect.

questions.q: An AMC proposes a change in the fundamental attributes of an open-ended scheme. Which of the following is required?
options: An exit window of not less than 30 days without exit load, with notice to unitholders and a public notice in an English national daily and a regional-language newspaper
Only an addendum on the AMC website
Approval of 75% of unitholders by postal ballot in every case
An exit window of 7 days with exit load applicable
questions.explanation: Fundamental change: addendum, public notice (English national daily + regional language paper), exit at prevailing NAV without load for ≥ 30 days; SID updated after the exit period.
hints: Correct — Regulation 22(9)(c) requires notice and a no-load exit option of at least 30 days.
Wrong — an addendum alone suffices only for other changes.
Wrong — 75% unitholder approval relates to removing the AMC.
Wrong — the exit window is at least 30 days and load-free.

questions.q: A distributor onboards a new woman investor (new PAN) from a B-30 city who invests through a ₹10,000 monthly SIP, totalling ₹1,20,000 in the first year. What additional commission can the distributor receive?
options: ₹2,400, as both B-30 and women incentives apply
₹1,200, claimed only once (no dual B-30 and women incentive)
₹2,000, the fixed cap for every eligible investor
Nil, because SIPs are not eligible
questions.explanation: Additional commission: 1% of first-year SIP or first lump sum (held ≥1 year), max ₹2,000; paid from the 2 bps investor-education set-aside; no dual incentive.
hints: Wrong — dual incentive is not allowed.
Correct — 1% of first-year SIP = ₹1,200 (below the ₹2,000 cap); dual incentives for the same investor are not permitted.
Wrong — ₹2,000 is a cap, not a fixed amount.
Wrong — SIPs are eligible (1% of first-year SIP).

questions.q: An open-ended equity-oriented scheme has daily net assets of ₹800 crore. What is the maximum base TER it can charge (annualised), in rupees?
options: ₹16.80 crore
₹15.20 crore
₹14.80 crore
₹16.05 crore
questions.explanation: TER slabs apply incrementally: first ₹500 cr 2.10%, next ₹250 cr 1.90%, next ₹1,250 cr 1.60% (equity-oriented).
hints: Wrong — that applies 2.10% to the entire ₹800 crore.
Wrong — that applies 1.90% throughout.
Wrong — that applies the non-equity 1.85% to the whole AUM.

questions.q: An investor buys units 2 months before the record date of a 1:1 bonus, and sells the original units 5 months after the record date at a loss. How is the loss treated?
options: It is ignored for set-off and treated as the cost of acquisition of the bonus units
It can be set off against salary income
It can be set off against any capital gain in the same year
It can be carried forward for 8 years and set off against STCG only
questions.explanation: Bonus stripping provision disallows the loss and adds it to the cost of the bonus units.
hints: Correct — bonus stripping: bought within 3 months before and sold within 9 months after the record date.
Wrong — capital losses never set off against salary.
Wrong — the loss is disallowed under bonus-stripping rules.
Wrong — the loss is disallowed, not carried forward.

questions.q: An investor submits a liquid fund purchase at 12.45 pm on Tuesday (a business day), but the money is credited to the scheme only at 2.30 pm the same day. Which NAV applies?
options: Closing NAV of Monday
Closing NAV of Wednesday
Tuesday's NAV only if the amount is below ₹2 lakh
Closing NAV of Tuesday — the day immediately preceding the next business day (Wednesday)
questions.explanation: Liquid funds: funds after 1.30 pm (same day) ⇒ closing NAV of the day immediately preceding the next business day; before cut-off ⇒ previous day's NAV.
hints: Wrong — Monday's NAV needs funds before the cut-off on Tuesday.
Wrong — Wednesday's NAV is not the rule for liquid funds.
Wrong — the ₹2 lakh distinction was removed from 1 Feb 2021.
Correct — funds became available after the 1.30 pm cut-off but on the same day, so the NAV of the day preceding the next business day applies.

questions.q: A scheme returned 14% against its tier-I benchmark's 11%. The standard deviation of the scheme's excess returns is 2%. What is its Information Ratio?
questions.explanation: Information Ratio = (Portfolio return − Benchmark return) ÷ SD of excess returns.
hints: Wrong — that is 11 ÷ 2.
Wrong — that is 14 ÷ 2.
Wrong — that inverts the ratio.

questions.q: Consider: I. The L.C. Gupta Committee was a 24-member committee. II. Stock futures were introduced in India before stock options. III. MSEI started trading in derivatives in February 2013. Which are correct?
options: I, II and III
I and III only
II and III only
I and II only
questions.explanation: Timeline: index futures Jun 2000, index options Jun 2001, stock options Jul 2001, stock futures Nov 2001; MSEI Feb 2013.
hints: Wrong — II is false.
Correct — stock options came in July 2001, stock futures in November 2001, so II is wrong.
Wrong — II is false and I is true.
Wrong — II is false and III is true.

questions.q: A free-float index has two stocks. A: 10 crore shares, base price ₹200, free-float factor 0.6. B: 5 crore shares, base price ₹400, free-float factor 0.5. Base value is 1,000. If A moves to ₹250 and B to ₹360, the new index value is closest to:
questions.explanation: Free-float index = (current FF mcap ÷ base FF mcap) × base value; FF mcap = shares × price × FF factor.
hints: Wrong — that uses full market cap (4,300 ÷ 4,000), ignoring free-float factors.
Wrong — that inverts the ratio (2,200 ÷ 2,400).
Wrong — that uses only stock A's 25% rise.

questions.q: Nifty spot is 20,000, the risk-free rate is 7% p.a. and the dividend yield is 1.5% p.a. Using continuous compounding, the fair price of 60-day Nifty futures is approximately:
questions.explanation: Continuous cost of carry: F = S·e^((r − q)T).
hints: Wrong — that ignores the dividend yield.
Wrong — that uses the discrete (1 + r − q)^T formula, a slightly different value.
Wrong — that uses only the dividend yield.

questions.q: A trader is short 4 near-month index futures, long 3 mid-month and long 2 far-month contracts. How are these positions treated?
options: 4 spreads and 1 naked mid-month long
3 near–mid calendar spreads, 1 near–far calendar spread and 1 naked far-month long
2 near–far spreads and 3 naked positions
All 9 contracts are naked positions
questions.explanation: Calendar spread positions are computed with respect to the near-month series; unmatched contracts are naked.
hints: Wrong — only 4 near-month shorts can pair, but the pairing is 3 mid + 1 far.
Correct — spreads are computed against the near month: 3 with mid, 1 with far; the remaining far-month long is naked.
Wrong — the workbook pairs mid first.
Wrong — offsetting positions form spreads.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹1,500. A 2-month European call with strike ₹1,520 is priced at ₹42; the risk-free rate is 7% p.a. (continuous). The fair price of the corresponding put by put-call parity is about:
questions.explanation: Put-call parity: C + X·e^(−rt) = P + S (European options only).
hints: Wrong — that ignores discounting of the strike.
Wrong — that subtracts the strike gap instead of adding.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.

questions.q: A call option has a delta of 0.45 and a gamma of 0.02. If the underlying rises by ₹5, the new delta is approximately:
questions.explanation: Gamma = change in delta per unit change in the underlying.
hints: Wrong — that adds gamma only once.
Wrong — delta rises, not falls, for a long call when price rises.
Wrong — that doubles the change.
Correct — change in delta = 0.02 × 5 = 0.10; new delta = 0.55.

questions.q: A trader buys a 1,000 put at ₹45 and sells a 950 put at ₹20 (same expiry). What are the break-even point and the maximum profit?
options: BEP ₹955; maximum profit ₹50
BEP ₹975; maximum profit ₹25
BEP ₹975; maximum profit ₹50
BEP ₹1,025; maximum profit ₹25
questions.explanation: Bear put spread: long higher-strike put, short lower-strike put; max loss = net debit; max profit = gap − debit; BEP = higher strike − debit.
hints: Wrong — mixes up debit and strike gap.
Correct — net debit 25; BEP = 1,000 − 25; max profit = 50 − 25.
Wrong — the strike gap must be reduced by the net debit.
Wrong — for puts the BEP is below the higher strike.

questions.q: Day 1: A buys 10 contracts from B. Day 2: C buys 15 from D. Day 3: A sells his 10 contracts to E (a new buyer). Day 4: C sells his 15 contracts to D, who was short. What is the open interest at the end of Day 4?
questions.explanation: OI rises when both sides open new positions, stays the same when a position is transferred, and falls when both sides close.
hints: Correct — Day 2 OI 25; Day 3 OI unchanged (E replaces A); Day 4 C and D both close out, so OI falls by 15 to 10.
Wrong — that was the OI after Day 2 and Day 3.
Wrong — that is the cumulative traded volume.
Wrong — E's long against B's short is still open.

questions.q: A 7.26% G-sec pays semi-annual coupons on 15 January and 15 July. Using 30/360, what is the accrued interest per ₹100 face value for settlement on 12 April?
questions.explanation: Accrued interest = annual coupon × day-count fraction; the workbook uses 30/360 for G-secs.
hints: Wrong — that uses Actual/365-style counting.
Wrong — that counts 90 days.
Wrong — that is the full half-year coupon.

questions.q: A bond has a dirty price of ₹102.40 and a modified duration of 7.2. Its PV01 per ₹100 face value is about:
questions.explanation: PV01 = Dirty price × MD ÷ 10,000.
hints: Wrong — off by a factor of 10.
Wrong — that is the price change for a 100 bp move.
Wrong — that ignores price.

questions.q: A call swaption gives the holder the right to:
options: Enter a swap as the payer of the fixed rate
Buy a government bond at a fixed price
Receive a cash payment whenever MIBOR exceeds a strike
Enter an interest rate swap as the receiver of the fixed rate
questions.explanation: Call swaption: right to receive fixed and pay floating; put swaption: right to pay fixed and receive floating.
hints: Wrong — that is a put (payer) swaption.
Wrong — that is a bond option.
Wrong — that is a caplet.
Correct — a call swaption = receiver swaption (receive fixed, pay floating).

questions.q: A G-sec has a clean price of ₹100.50 and accrued interest of ₹1.20 to the spot settlement date. Financing cost is 6% p.a. (Actual/365) for 30 days on the dirty price. Accrued interest from the last coupon to the futures settlement date is ₹1.80. The theoretical futures clean price is closest to:
questions.explanation: Bond futures price = cash (dirty) price + financing cost − income on cash position.
hints: Wrong — that is the futures dirty price before deducting income.
Correct — dirty 101.70 + financing 101.70 × 6% × 30/365 (0.50) = 102.20; less income on cash position 1.80 = 100.40.
Wrong — that ignores the income on cash position.
Wrong — that subtracts financing.

questions.q: A trader buys 10 lots of overnight MIBOR futures at 6.50% and squares off at 6.60%. Ignoring costs, the profit is:
questions.explanation: MIBOR futures: ₹411 per bp per lot; long gains when the rate rises.
hints: Wrong — that is for 1 lot.
Wrong — that uses the tick value instead of bp value.
Wrong — off by a factor of 10.

questions.q: Which statement about exchange-traded interest rate options on GOI securities is NOT correct?
options: The strike price interval is ₹0.25
They can be exercised on any trading day before expiry
One lot represents bonds of face value ₹2 lakh
Final settlement uses the weighted average price of the underlying in the last two hours on NDS-OM
questions.explanation: Exchange IROs: premium-style European; lot FV ₹2 lakh; strike interval ₹0.25; cash settled T+1.
hints: Wrong — this is a correct specification.
Correct — this is the incorrect statement — they are European options, exercisable only on expiry.
Wrong — this is correct.
Wrong — this is correct.

questions.q: A fund holds a ₹50 crore G-sec portfolio with modified duration 5.5. Bond futures trade at ₹99.20 with a modified duration of 4.8. How many lots are needed to hedge the portfolio fully?
options: About 2,500 lots
About 3,437 lots
About 2,888 lots
About 2,302 lots
questions.explanation: Duration-based hedge lots = (MD_p × Value) ÷ (MD_f × Futures price × 2,000).
hints: Wrong — that is face value ÷ ₹2 lakh, ignoring duration.
Wrong — that inverts the duration ratio.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.
